ideas.hypothesis: Fines deter state-owned enterprises less than private firms, because soft budget constraints and political backing blunt the financial penalty. As a result, SOEs re-offend more often after an equivalent sanction.
ideas.test: Coded decisions of one or two competition authorities (e.g., Indonesia, Korea) over 15 years. Use a survival model of time to a second infringement, comparing state-owned and private firms and controlling for fine size and sector.
ideas.disconfirming: SOEs re-offend at the same rate as or a lower rate than comparable private firms after similar fines.

ideas.hypothesis: Wider access to follow-on antitrust damages lowers leniency applications, because applicants expect higher civil liability. The drop is smaller where leniency recipients are shielded from joint and several liability.
ideas.test: Panel of leniency application counts reported by EU member state authorities before and after national damages-law reforms. Run difference-in-differences by whether the reform shields leniency recipients from joint and several liability.
ideas.disconfirming: Leniency applications do not fall after damages reforms, or the effect does not depend on the shield.

ideas.hypothesis: In bid-rigging cases, economic and circumstantial evidence such as bid patterns is enough to meet the standard of proof more often than in other price-fixing cases. Tender data are less ambiguous than market price data.
ideas.test: Code cartel decisions and appeals in one jurisdiction (e.g., India) by evidence type and outcome. Logit of the infringement being upheld on appeal, interacting evidence type with case type.
ideas.disconfirming: Cases resting only on economic evidence survive appeal no more often in bid rigging than in other cartel cases.

ideas.hypothesis: Reintroducing criminal sanctions for cartels in Chile raised leniency applications and cartel detections in the following years.
ideas.test: Annual counts of cartel investigations, leniency applications and convictions from the Chilean agency's reports, before and after the criminal reform. Interrupted time series, with a regional jurisdiction without criminalization as comparison.
ideas.disconfirming: Leniency applications and detections do not change after criminalization.

ideas.hypothesis: Criminal cartel prosecutions that rely mainly on circumstantial evidence fail more often than administrative cases built on the same kind of evidence, because the criminal standard of proof is higher.
ideas.test: Code cartel matters in jurisdictions that run both criminal and administrative tracks (e.g., UK, US, Czech Republic) by evidence type and outcome. Compare conviction or infringement rates by track and evidence type.
ideas.disconfirming: Cases resting on circumstantial evidence fail at similar rates on both tracks.

ideas.hypothesis: Publishing detailed fining guidelines lowers the share of fines appealed and the size of fine reductions on appeal, because sanctions become more predictable.
ideas.test: Fine decisions and appeal outcomes in Serbia and a few other authorities before and after fining guidelines were adopted. Regress appeal incidence and percentage reduction on a post-guidelines indicator.
ideas.disconfirming: Appeal rates and fine reductions stay the same or rise after guidelines are published.

ideas.hypothesis: Authorities that adopt formal procedural fairness safeguards, such as access to file and a hearing officer, receive more leniency applications, because firms trust the agency to keep its promises.
ideas.test: Cross-country panel of leniency applications from authority annual reports, with timing of procedural safeguard adoption coded from the international recommendations. Fixed-effects regression.
ideas.disconfirming: Leniency applications are unrelated to, or fall after, procedural safeguard adoption.

ideas.hypothesis: Jurisdictions with stronger due process guarantees in investigations impose lower nominal fines but see fewer of them annulled on appeal.
ideas.test: Cross-jurisdiction dataset of cartel and abuse fines and appeal outcomes, merged with a due process index coded from comparative studies.
ideas.disconfirming: Due process strength is unrelated to fine levels or appeal success.

ideas.hypothesis: Competition Commission of India orders where parties raised procedural objections, such as the right to cross-examine or inadequate notice, are set aside or remanded on appeal far more often than orders without such objections.
ideas.test: Code all CCI final orders and appellate decisions over ten years for procedural objections and outcomes. Logit of set-aside or remand.
ideas.disconfirming: Procedural objections do not predict appellate reversal.

ideas.hypothesis: Incumbent telecom operators that challenge competition authorities' jurisdiction through statutory interpretation arguments delay final rulings substantially, even when they lose the challenge.
ideas.test: Compare the time from complaint to final decision for telecom cases with and without jurisdictional challenges across several jurisdictions (South Africa, New Zealand, others).
ideas.disconfirming: Jurisdictional challenges do not lengthen case duration.

ideas.hypothesis: Germany's provisions targeting excessive energy pricing lowered retail energy margins and raised consumer welfare without reducing supplier entry.
ideas.test: Regional retail electricity and gas margins and supplier counts in Germany before and after the excessive-pricing provision, compared with a neighboring country. Difference-in-differences.
ideas.disconfirming: Margins do not fall, or entry falls significantly.

ideas.hypothesis: Private competition claims in pharmaceuticals settle at higher rates and amounts than in other sectors, because purchasers can quantify overcharges from generic-delay conduct.
ideas.test: UK competition litigation dataset including settlements (as compiled in the source). Compare settlement incidence and disclosed amounts for pharmaceutical and other sectors.
ideas.disconfirming: Pharmaceutical claims settle no more often and for no larger amounts than claims in other sectors.

ideas.hypothesis: Civil law jurisdictions award antitrust damages less often than common law ones, because their procedures lack disclosure and aggregate litigation. The gap narrows after harmonized damages rules are adopted.
ideas.test: Compile competition damages judgments by member state over 1999-2019. Count regression on legal origin, interacted with the post-harmonization period.
ideas.disconfirming: Damages awards show no legal-origin gap, or the gap does not narrow.

ideas.hypothesis: GCC states that adopted leniency programs open more cartel investigations than GCC states that rely only on advocacy and ex officio detection.
ideas.test: Cartel investigations by year from GCC authority reports, coded for leniency adoption dates. Event-study comparison across member states.
ideas.disconfirming: Cartel investigations do not rise after leniency adoption.

ideas.hypothesis: Historically, cartels lasted longer in jurisdictions where freedom of contract let courts enforce restrictive agreements, and cartel duration fell once competition statutes made such agreements unenforceable.
ideas.test: Historical case records of Canadian cartels before and after the 1889 statute, coded for duration and breakdowns caused by cheating.
ideas.disconfirming: Cartel duration does not fall after agreements became unenforceable.

ideas.hypothesis: When competition authorities strike down professional association bans on advertising and promotion, member entry and non-price competition (opening hours, services offered) increase.
ideas.test: Pharmacy registers and service-attribute data in Polish regions before and after the decision against the chemists' chamber, compared with regions or professions not affected.
ideas.disconfirming: Entry and non-price attributes do not change.

ideas.hypothesis: Fines are reduced on appeal more often where one administrative agency both investigates and imposes the sanction than where a separate tribunal or court imposes it.
ideas.test: Cross-jurisdiction appeal outcomes for competition fines, coded by institutional design (integrated agency versus prosecutorial model).
ideas.disconfirming: Appeal reduction rates do not differ by institutional design.

ideas.hypothesis: Newer competition regimes that harmonize with EU or US models converge to a holistic, cumulative assessment of circumstantial evidence within a few years of adopting their laws.
ideas.test: Code cartel decisions from several Asian authorities for item-by-item versus holistic evidence reasoning. Track the share of holistic reasoning over time since the law was adopted.
ideas.disconfirming: No convergence toward holistic assessment over time.

ideas.hypothesis: Fining guidelines that make parent companies liable for subsidiaries' infringements raise the average fine and reduce repeat infringements in the corporate group.
ideas.test: Compare fines and group-level recidivism before and after parental-liability provisions in fining guidelines.
ideas.disconfirming: Fines and group recidivism do not change.

ideas.hypothesis: Incumbent postal operators that keep a reserved universal-service area price competitive parcel services below incremental cost more often than incumbents without a reserved area, using cross-subsidies.
ideas.test: Cost-allocation data from regulatory accounts of several European postal incumbents, with competitive-segment prices compared against incremental cost estimates, split by reserved-area status.
ideas.disconfirming: Below-cost pricing is no more frequent among incumbents with reserved areas.

ideas.hypothesis: Private enforcement plays almost no role in Sub-Saharan African competition regimes; the few private claims follow public decisions rather than standing alone.
ideas.test: Count private competition suits in court records of Kenya, Zambia and South Africa over 15 years, classifying each as follow-on or stand-alone.
ideas.disconfirming: Stand-alone private claims are common.

ideas.hypothesis: Incumbent operators in regulated industries raise procedural-fairness challenges more often than other respondents and use them to delay remedies.
ideas.test: Code procedural challenges in competition proceedings by respondent type (incumbent versus other) in one or two jurisdictions. Compare their frequency and the resulting delay.
ideas.disconfirming: Incumbents raise procedural challenges no more often than other respondents.

ideas.hypothesis: Dominant firms use long-term exclusive contracts with high liquidated damages for breach to foreclose rivals. Competition intervention against such contracts increases entry.
ideas.test: Case studies coded from abuse decisions involving exclusive contracts, with market entry measured before and after the remedy.
ideas.disconfirming: Entry does not rise after the contracts are struck down.

ideas.hypothesis: Courts applying a rule-of-reason analysis to exemptions for public service providers uphold fewer exemptions than courts that read the statutory exemptions literally.
ideas.test: Code court decisions on public-service competition exemptions across several jurisdictions by interpretive approach and outcome.
ideas.disconfirming: Exemption outcomes do not differ by interpretive approach.

ideas.hypothesis: Fines and detection rates in East African Community member states are too low to deter cartels, so expected penalties fall below estimated overcharges.
ideas.test: Compile fines and investigation counts from EAC member authorities. Calibrate expected penalty (detection probability x fine) against standard overcharge estimates.
ideas.disconfirming: Expected penalties exceed typical cartel gains.

ideas.hypothesis: Private suits against administrative monopoly conduct by government bodies rarely succeed compared with suits against private firms, because courts defer to the state.
ideas.test: Code private competition judgments in one jurisdiction by defendant type (government body versus private firm) and outcome.
ideas.disconfirming: Success rates are similar across defendant types.

ideas.hypothesis: Member states of regional economic communities that adopt regional competition rules are more likely to repeal national exemptions for export cartels.
ideas.test: Cross-country dataset of export cartel exemptions and membership in regional competition regimes. Hazard model of repeal.
ideas.disconfirming: Repeal is unrelated to regional integration.

ideas.hypothesis: Public tenders run by government-owned enterprises in Indonesia are found to involve bid rigging more often than tenders run by line ministries.
ideas.test: Code Indonesian competition authority tender decisions by procuring entity type and infringement finding. Compare infringement rates.
ideas.disconfirming: Infringement rates are similar or lower for tenders run by government-owned enterprises.

ideas.hypothesis: Competition authorities define narrower, molecule-level markets in pharmaceutical abuse cases than in pharmaceutical merger cases, and narrower definitions are associated with infringement findings.
ideas.test: Code market definitions in pharmaceutical abuse and merger decisions of the European Commission and several national authorities.
ideas.disconfirming: Market breadth does not differ between abuse and merger cases.

ideas.hypothesis: Raising administrative surcharges under an anti-monopoly law reduces private damages claims, because public sanctions substitute for private ones.
ideas.test: Korean court records of private damages suits alongside annual surcharge levels. Time-series regression.
ideas.disconfirming: Private claims rise or are unaffected when surcharges rise.
